question:
A rigid body is made of three identical thin rods, each of length L fastened together in the form of the letter H. The body is free to rotate about a horizontal axis that runs along the length of one of the legs of the H. The body is allowed to fall from rest from a position in which the plane of the H is horizontal.

What is the angular speed of the body when the plane of H is vertical $\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$
solution:
Let the mass of each identical thin rod be m and length be L .

Total mass of the system $=3 \mathrm{~m}$.

For rod 1 which is lying along the axis of rotation, all its mass lies on the axis of rotation. So, its moment of inertia about this axis is $\mathrm{I}_1=0$

For rod 2 which is perpendicular crossbar of length L has one end on the axis of rotation and extends perpendicularly to distance L. So, its moment of inertia is $\mathrm{I}_2=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~mL}^2$

For rod 3 which is parallel at distance L from the axis, every mass element of this rod is at a constant perpendicular distance $\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{L}$ from the axis of rotation.

\mathrm{I}_3=\int \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{dm}=\mathrm{L}^2 \int \mathrm{dm}=\mathrm{mL}^2

Total moment of inertia is,

I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 = 0 + \frac{1}{3}mL^2 + mL^2 = \frac{4}{3}mL^2

Initially the letter H is in the horizontal position and at rest.

Centre of mass of rod 1 is on the axis (height = 0).

Centre of mass of rod 2 is at distance $\frac{L}{2}$ from the axis.

Centre of mass of rod 3 is at distance $L$ from the axis.

Position of Centre of mass of the entire system is,

h_{\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{m(0)\; +\; m\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)\; +\; m(L)}{m\; +\; m\; +\; m} = \frac{\frac{3}{2}mL}{3m} = \frac{L}{2}

When the body falls from the horizontal position to the vertical position, its Centre of mass drops by a vertical height:

\Delta h = h_{\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{L}{2}

Loss in potential energy of the system is

\Delta U = (\text{Total Mass})g \times \Delta h = (3m)g\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{3}{2}mgL

Since the system starts from rest, initial kinetic energy is $K_i = 0$.

By energy conservation, the loss in potential energy equals the gain in rotational kinetic energy ($K_f$):

K_f = \Delta U

The rotational kinetic energy of a body rotating with angular speed $\omega$ is $K_f = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$

Substituting the expression for moment of inertia $I = \frac{4}{3}mL^2$ and $\Delta U = \frac{3}{2}mgL$:

\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}mL^2\right)\omega^2 = \frac{3}{2}mgL

\frac{2}{3}mL^2\,\omega^2 = \frac{3}{2}mgL

\frac{2}{3}L\,\omega^2 = \frac{3}{2}g

\omega^2 = \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{3g}{2L} = \frac{9g}{4L}

\omega = \sqrt{\frac{9g}{4L}} = \frac{3}{2}\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}

Therefore, the angular speed of the body when the plane of H is vertical is $\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

question: A uniform circular disc A of radius $r$ is made from a metal plate of thickness $t$ and another uniform circular disc B of radius $4r$ is made from the same metal plate of thickness $t/4$. If equal torques act on the discs A and B, initially both being at rest. At a later instant, the angular speeds of a point on the rim of A and another point on the rim of B are $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ respectively. We have
options: the relation depends on the actual magnitude of the torques.
solution:
Let the density of the metal plate is $\rho$

If the radius of circular disc is r and of thickness t, then the volume of circular disc is $\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{At}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{t}$.

Then mass of a uniform disc is $\mathrm{m}=\rho \mathrm{V}=\pi \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{t} \rho$

For disc A radius is r , and thickness t , mass is

m_A = \rho\, \pi\, r^2\, t

For disc B radius is $4r$, and thickness $\frac{t}{4}$, mass is

m_B = \rho\, \pi\, (4r)^2\left(\frac{t}{4}\right) = \rho\, \pi\, (16\, r^2)\left(\frac{t}{4}\right) = 4\, \rho\, \pi\, r^2\, t = 4\, m_A

The moment of inertia of disc (or cylinder) of mass $m$ and radius $r$ about an axis passing through the Centre is

I = \frac{1}{2}mr^2

Moment of inertia of disc A is $I_A = \frac{1}{2}m_A\, r^2$

Moment of inertia of disc B is

I_B = \frac{1}{2}m_B(4r)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(4m_A)(16r^2) = 32\, m_A r^2 = 64\, I_A

Using Newton's second law for rotation, torque $\tau$ relates to angular acceleration $\alpha$ by:

\tau = I\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{\tau}{I}

Since both discs start from rest ($\omega_0 = 0$) under equal torque $\tau$ for time $t$:

\omega = \alpha t = \frac{\tau t}{I}

So, final angular speed of disc A is $\omega_A = \frac{\tau t}{I_A}$

And the final angular speed of disc B is $\omega_B = \frac{\tau t}{I_B} = \frac{\tau t}{64 I_A}$

\Rightarrow \omega_A = 64\, \omega_B \Rightarrow \omega_A > \omega_B

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

q: Two men support a uniform horizontal rod at its two ends. If one of them suddenly lets go, the force exerted by the rod on the other man just after this moment will :
question: Two men support a uniform horizontal rod at its two ends. If one of them suddenly lets go, the force exerted by the rod on the other man just after this moment will :
options: become unequal to the force exerted by him on the rod.
solution:
Let the uniform horizontal rod have mass m and length L .

Initially, two men support the rod symmetrically at its two ends A and B.

Downward gravitational force acts at the Centre of mass is $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg}$.

By symmetry, each man exerts an upward normal force $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A} 0}=\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{B} 0}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{2}$

As soon as end B is released, the rod begins to rotate about the remaining support point at end A.

At this instantaneous moment, the rod is still horizontal $(\theta=0)$.

Let $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$ be the new upward vertical force exerted by the remaining support at end A on the rod.

The moment of inertia of rod about end A is $\mathrm{I}=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~mL}^2$

Taking torque about end A is $\tau_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}} \alpha$

The only force causing torque about end A is weight mg acting at the Centre of mass which is at distance $\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$ from A:

\tau_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{mg}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~L}}{2}\right)

\Rightarrow mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{3}mL^2\right)\alpha

\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)}{\frac{1}{3}mL^2}=\frac{3g}{2L}

The Centre of mass is located at distance $r=\frac{L}{2}$ from the pivot end A.

Since angular velocity $\omega=0$ at $t=0^{+}$, centripetal acceleration is zero.

The downward linear acceleration of the Centre of mass is tangential:

a_{\mathrm{cm}}=\alpha\times\frac{L}{2}=\left(\frac{3g}{2L}\right)\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)=\frac{3}{4}g

Applying Newton's second law for vertical motion of the Centre of mass:

F_{\mathrm{net},y}=m\cdot a_{\mathrm{cm}}

mg-N_A=m\left(\frac{3}{4}g\right)

N_A=mg-\frac{3}{4}mg=\frac{1}{4}mg

Initial force exerted by the rod on the man $N_{A0}=\frac{1}{2}mg=0.50mg$.

Force exerted immediately after release $N_A=\frac{1}{4}mg=0.25mg$.

Since $0.25mg\lt 0.50mg$, the force decreases.

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

q: A uniform metre stick is held vertically with one end on the floor and is allowed to fall. The speed of the other end when it hits the floor assuming that the end at the floor does not slip :
question: A uniform metre stick is held vertically with one end on the floor and is allowed to fall. The speed of the other end when it hits the floor assuming that the end at the floor does not slip :
solution:
A metre stick has length $\mathrm{L}=1 \mathrm{~m}$.

Mass of the metre stick $=\mathrm{m}$.

Initially the stick is vertical, so the initial angle with horizontal is $\theta_{\mathrm{i}}=90^{\circ}$

Finally the stick is horizontal, so the final angle with horizontal is $\theta_{\mathrm{f}}=0^{\circ}$ just before hitting the floor.

Centre of mass of a uniform rod of length L is at height $\mathrm{h}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$.

Initial height of Centre of mass, $\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$.

Final height of Centre of mass when flat on floor, $\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{f}}=0$.

Loss in potential energy is $\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{mg}\left(\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{i}}-\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{f}}\right)=\mathrm{mg}\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}\right)$

The bottom end at the floor acts as a fixed pivot (no slipping). So, the moment of inertia of stick about the fixed end is

I = \frac{1}{3}mL^2

Gain in rotational kinetic energy at angular speed $\omega$:

K_f = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}mL^2\right)\omega^2 = \frac{1}{6}mL^2\omega^2

Assuming no non-conservative work is done, the total mechanical energy of stick remains unchanged.

\Delta U = K_f

mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{6}mL^2\omega^2

\frac{gL}{2} = \frac{L^2\omega^2}{6}

\omega^2 = \frac{6gL}{2L^2} = \frac{3g}{L}

\omega = \sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}

The top end is at distance $r = L$ from the bottom pivoted end.

Linear speed $v$ is given by $v = \omega L$:

v = \sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}} \times L = \sqrt{3gL}

Since it is a metre stick, length $L = 1\ \mathrm{m}$:

v = \sqrt{3g(1)} = \sqrt{3g}

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

q: A light rod of length 1 m pivoted at its centre and two masses of 5 kg and 2 kg are hung from the ends as shown in figure. Assuming that it was horizontal in the beginning, the initial angular acceleration of the rod is [g = 10 m/s2]
question: A light rod of length 1 m pivoted at its centre and two masses of 5 kg and 2 kg are hung from the ends as shown in figure. Assuming that it was horizontal in the beginning, the initial angular acceleration of the rod is [g = 10 m/s2]
solution:
Length of the light rod, $L = 1 ext{ m}$, pivoted at centre of the rod

Distance of each mass from central pivot, $r = \frac{L}{2} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 ext{ m}$

Left mass, $m_1 = 2 kg$

Right mass, $m_2 = 5 kg$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10m/s^2$

Since the rod is light (negligible mass), the moment of inertia is of the two point masses attached at its ends:

I = m_1 r^2 + m_2 r^2 = (m_1 + m_2)r^2

Substituting $m_1 = 2kg$, $m_2 = 5 kg$, and $r = 0.5 m$:

I = (2 + 5) \times (0.5)^2 = 7 \times 0.25 = 1.75\text{ kg} \cdot \text{m}^2

Let the clockwise torque is negative and anti-clockwise torque is positive.

Torque produced by 2 kg mass about pivot point is counter-clockwise (positive).

\tau_1 = m_1 g \times r = 2 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 10\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}

Torque produced by 5 kg mass about pivot point is clockwise (negative).

\tau_2 = -m_2 g \times r = -5 \times 10 \times 0.5 = -25\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}

Net torque acting on the rod:

\tau_{\mathrm{net}} = \tau_1 + \tau_2 = 10 - 25 = -15\ \mathrm{N\cdot m}

So, the magnitude of initial angular acceleration of rod is 15Nm

Using Newton's second law for rotation:

\tau_{\mathrm{net}} = I \cdot \alpha

\alpha = \frac{\tau_{\mathrm{net}}}{I} = \frac{15}{1.75} = \frac{60}{7}\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}

\alpha \approx 8.5714\ \mathrm{rad/s^2} \approx 8.6\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

question: In the arrangement shown in figure, two equal masses hung from light cords wrapped around a uniform solid cylinder of mass M and radius R. The cylinder is free to rotate about a horizontal axis. If the system is released from rest, then, the linear acceleration of each mass is
solution:
Let the cylinder have mass M and radius R .

As the system releases from rest, both masses move downward together with a linear acceleration a.

The unwinding cords cause the cylinder to rotate with angular acceleration $\alpha$.

Let the tension in each of the two vertical cords be T.

The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder of mass M and radius R about its central axis is

\mathrm{I}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{R}^2

Each mass m experiences a downward gravitational force mg and an upward tension force T .

Using Newton's second law $\left(\mathrm{F}_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{m} \mathrm{a}\right)$ for one mass:

\mathrm{mg}-\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{ma} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{a})

Since there are two identical masses, the total upward force acting on the cylinder from both cords is 2T.

The magnitude of torque due to each cord on the cylinder is $\tau=\mathrm{T} \cdot \mathrm{R}$ on the outer edge of the cylinder in the same direction of rotation.

Total torque acting on the cylinder:

\tau_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{TR}+\mathrm{TR}=2 \mathrm{TR}

Using Newton's second law for rotation ($\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha$):

2TR = I\alpha

Since the cords unwind without slipping, the linear acceleration $a$ of the downward moving masses is related with the angular acceleration $\alpha$ of the cylinder:

a = \alpha R \Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{a}{R}

Substituting $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$ and $\alpha = \frac{a}{R}$ into the torque equation:

2TR = \left(\frac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\left(\frac{a}{R}\right) = \frac{1}{2}Ma

\Rightarrow T = \frac{1}{4}Ma \Rightarrow m(g-a) = \frac{1}{4}Ma

mg - ma = \frac{1}{4}Ma

mg = ma + \frac{1}{4}Ma = a\left(m + \frac{M}{4}\right) = a\left(\frac{4m+M}{4}\right)

a = \frac{4mg}{M+4m}

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

solution:
Rotational power generated by a torque $\tau$ acting on a body rotating with angular velocity $\omega(t)$ is the work done

\omega(t)=\omega_0+\alpha t=\alpha t=\left(\frac{\tau}{I}\right)t

Substituting the expression for $\omega(t)$ into the power equation:

solution:
A uniform rod of mass m and total length L is hinged at one end.

Initially, the rod lies horizontally at rest $\left(\omega_0=0\right)$ along the boundary line dividing the space.

Above the broken line gravity is active (g downwards).

Below the broken line there is no gravity $(\mathrm{g}=0)$.

As the rod falls from the horizontal position to the vertical position, its Centre of mass moves downwards from the horizontal boundary line through a total vertical distance of $\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$.

Only the upper half of the region has gravity acting on the mass elements.

The moment of inertia (I) about hinge is $\mathrm{I}=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~L}^2$

Initially the rod is released from rest, so the initial kinetic energy is $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{i}}=0$

Considering a small element of the rod of length dx at distance x from the hinge $(0 \leq \mathrm{x} \leq \mathrm{L})$.

Mass of the element is $\mathrm{dm}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{L}}\right) \mathrm{dx}$

When the rod rotates by 90° to become vertical, the element at distance x drops vertically by distance $\mathrm{h}(\mathrm{x})=\mathrm{x}$.

If $\mathrm{x} \leq \frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$ the element stays above the broken line, i.e., in the gravity region and the vertical distance fallen in gravity region $=\mathrm{x}$.

If $x \gt \frac{L}{2}$, the element enters the no-gravity region below height $\frac{L}{2}$, vertical distance fallen within the gravity region = $\frac{L}{2}$.

So, potential energy lost by all elements in the gravitational field:

question: A uniform thin rod of mass $M$ and length Lis supported horizontally by two supports, one at each end. At time $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{0}$, the left support is removed. Normal force on the right support immediately after the left support is removed is $\frac{M g}{x}$. Find $x$.
solution:
Let the uniform thin rod have mass M , length L , and be pivoted at its right end support $\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{L})$.

Immediately after the left support at $\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{x}=0)$ is removed :

Downward gravitational force Mg acting at its Centre of mass $\left(\mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}\right)$.

Upward normal reaction force $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}$ exerted by the right support at $\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{L})$.

The rod begins to rotate about the right end support B.

The weight $Mg$ acts at a distance of $\frac{L}{2}$ from B.

\tau_B = Mg \times \left(\frac{L}{2}\right)

The moment of inertia of for a uniform thin rod about an axis passing through one end perpendicular to its length is

I_B = \frac{1}{3} M L^2

Using Newton's second law for rotation ($\tau_B = I_B\alpha$):

Mg \times \left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{3} M L^2\right)\alpha

\alpha = \frac{Mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)}{\frac{1}{3} M L^2} = \frac{3g}{2L}

The linear vertical acceleration of the Centre of mass ($a_{\mathrm{com}}$) is related to the angular acceleration $\alpha$ by:

a_{\mathrm{com}} = r\alpha

where $r = \frac{L}{2}$ is the distance from the pivot B to the Centre of mass.

a_{\mathrm{com}} = \left(\frac{L}{2}\right) \times \alpha = \left(\frac{L}{2}\right) \times \left(\frac{3g}{2L}\right) = \frac{3}{4}g

Applying Newton's second law for vertical translation of the Centre of mass:

\sum\limits F_y = M a_{\mathrm{com}}

Mg - N_B' = M a_{\mathrm{com}}

Mg - N'_B = M \times \left(\frac{3}{4}g\right)

N'_B = Mg - \frac{3}{4}Mg

N'_B = \frac{1}{4}Mg = \frac{Mg}{4}

\Rightarrow N'_B = \frac{Mg}{x} = \frac{Mg}{4} \Rightarrow x = 4

Therefore, the value of x is 4.

q: A uniform cylinder of radius $\mathbf{R}(=\mathbf{3 m})$ is spun about its axis at an angular velocity $\omega_0(=40 \sqrt{\pi} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s})$ and placed between two perpendicular walls. The coefficient of friction between the walls and cylinder is $\mu(=0.2)$. If this cylinder makes $N$ turns before it stops, then find the value of $N$.
question: A uniform cylinder of radius $\mathbf{R}(=\mathbf{3 m})$ is spun about its axis at an angular velocity $\omega_0(=40 \sqrt{\pi} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s})$ and placed between two perpendicular walls. The coefficient of friction between the walls and cylinder is $\mu(=0.2)$. If this cylinder makes $N$ turns before it stops, then find the value of $N$.
solution:
Let $\mathrm{N}_1$ be the normal force exerted by the vertical wall and $\mathrm{N}_2$ be the normal force exerted by the horizontal floor.

As the cylinder spins counter-clockwise, kinetic friction forces oppose its motion at both contact surfaces:

Friction force at the vertical wall is $\mathrm{f}_1=\mu \mathrm{N}_1$

Friction force at the horizontal floor is $\mathrm{f}_2=\mu \mathrm{N}_2$

Since the cylinder remains stationary at the corner while spinning:

Net horizontal force is zero,

\sum F_x = N_1 - f_2 = 0 \Rightarrow N_1 = \mu N_2 \ldots (i)

Net vertical force is zero,

\sum F_y = N_2 + f_1 - Mg = 0 \Rightarrow N_2 + \mu N_1 = Mg \ldots (ii)

Substituting $N_1 = \mu N_2$ into equation (ii):

N_2 + \mu(\mu N_2) = Mg

N_2(1+\mu^2) = Mg \Rightarrow N_2 = \frac{Mg}{1+\mu^2}

Then substituting $N_2$ back to find $N_1$,

N_1 = \frac{\mu Mg}{1+\mu^2}

Both friction forces exert retarding torques in the same sense to slow down the cylinder's rotation:

\tau_{\text{net}} = f_1R + f_2R = \mu N_1 R + \mu N_2 R = \mu R(N_1 + N_2)

\tau_{\text{net}} = \mu R\left(\frac{\mu Mg}{1+\mu^2} + \frac{Mg}{1+\mu^2}\right) = \frac{\mu(1+\mu)MgR}{1+\mu^2}

The moment of inertia of a solid uniform cylinder about its central axis is:

I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2

Using Newton's second law for rotation ($\tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha$) :

\frac{\mu(1+\mu)MgR}{1+\mu^2}=\left(\frac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\alpha

\alpha=\frac{2\mu(1+\mu)g}{(1+\mu^2)R}

The coefficient of kinetic friction is $\mu=0.2$, the radius of cylinder is $R=3\ \mathrm{m}$ and acceleration due to gravity is $g=10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$

Substituting these values:

\alpha=\frac{2\times0.2\times(1+0.2)\times10}{(1+0.2^2)\times3}=\frac{0.4\times1.2\times10}{1.04\times3}=\frac{4.8}{3.12}=\frac{20\,\mathrm{rad}}{13\,\mathrm{s^2}}

Using the third rotational equation of motion ($\omega^2=\omega_0^2-2\alpha\theta$):

0=\omega_0^2-2\alpha\theta \rightarrow \theta=\frac{\omega_0^2}{2\alpha}

Given $\omega_0=40\sqrt{\pi}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$:

\theta=\frac{1600\pi}{2\times\left(\frac{20}{13}\right)}=\frac{1600\pi\times13}{40}=520\pi\ \mathrm{rad}

Since 1 complete turn $=2\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$:

N=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}=\frac{520\pi}{2\pi}=260

Therefore, the cylinder makes 260 turns before stopping.
